title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: one change or two, and how far back the tense goes

questions.prompt: Your book asks whether "They will become more and more substantial" expresses a gradual increase or decrease, a parallel change, or a comparison of superiority. Which is it, and how do you decide?

options.text: A parallel change, because two comparatives appear.
A parallel change, because the sentence looks to the future.
A comparison of superiority, because more is used.
A gradual increase, because one thing changes steadily.

questions.explanation: Count the things that change: only the brain does, and it does so steadily in one direction, which is a gradual increase. A parallel change needs two changes tied to each other by a doubled the, as in the more you read the more you know, and this sentence has no second clause at all — the repetition of more belongs to the structure itself, not to two separate comparisons. A comparison of superiority would need something to compare with, introduced by than, and nothing here is being outdone. And a sentence being in the future changes nothing: all three structures work in every tense.

questions.prompt: Direct speech: "I have already finished my project, and I must hand it in today." Which reported version is right?

options.text: She said that she has already finished her project and she must hand it in today.
She said that she had already finished her project and had to hand it in that day.
She told that she had already finished her project and she must hand it in that same day.
She said that she finished her project and she had to hand it in the next day.

questions.explanation: Three shifts are needed at once and only one version makes all three: the present perfect steps back to the past perfect, must becomes had to, and today becomes that day. Keeping the present perfect and must leaves two of the three shifts undone. Leaving must unchanged is the commonest of the three errors, because must has no past form of its own and pupils forget that had to supplies it — and told that fails in any case, since told needs a person after it. And turning the present perfect into a plain past loses the already, while the next day names a different day from the one she meant.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the wrong structure for what it wants to say?

options.text: The more he practises every single evening, the better he plays.
His playing is getting better and better.
The better and better he practises, the more he plays.
The less he practises, the worse he plays.

questions.explanation: The third sentence mixes the two structures: it puts the doubled better and better inside the frame that belongs to the doubled the, so each half now carries a structure of its own and neither works. The first and the fourth are correct parallel changes, one rising and one falling, and they show that the frame does not care about direction. The second is a correct gradual change, describing one thing moving steadily. Keep the two apart by counting: one change takes better and better, two linked changes take the more and the better.

questions.prompt: Your book asks you to sort the four readers of Lesson 25 into for and against. Why is Manel's message the one that resists?

options.text: Because she does not mention the internet at all.
Because she recounts a harm and defends a need at once.
Because her message is shorter than the others.
Because she writes about somebody else and not herself.

questions.explanation: Manel loses her engagement because of the time she spends online, which reads as a warning, and she ends by saying she could not stop because she needs to feel closer to the rest of the world, which reads as a defence. Both are in the same message, so either column betrays half of it. The internet is in fact her whole subject, from the meeting in cyberspace to the chatting that broke the engagement. Length has nothing to do with it, and the message is not notably short. And she writes about her own life throughout — the reader who writes about somebody else is Ian, whose subject is his wife.

questions.prompt: A pupil is sorting words by stress and hesitates over three of them. Which row is entirely correct?

options.text: MEDicine · eduCAtion · environMENtal
mediCINE · EDucation · enVIronmental
MEDicine · EDucation · environMENtal
mediCINE · eduCAtion · ENvironmental

questions.explanation: medicine carries its stress on the first syllable, while education and environmental both end in a suffix that pulls the stress towards it — the syllable immediately before -tion gives eduCAtion, and the same pattern before -al gives environMENtal, its fourth. Any row that stresses the final syllable of medicine invents a pattern English does not use for this word. Any row that stresses the first syllable of education ignores the strongest rule of the exercise. And stressing the first syllable of environmental would leave the word four syllables long with its weight at the wrong end.

questions.prompt: The recording lists everything that will change about future man: taller, larger forehead, stronger eyes, weaker limbs, more sensitive fingers, no hair. How does the speaker end?

options.text: By saying that future man will not really be a human being at all.
By listing one more change, to the voice.
By admitting that none of it can really be predicted at all.
By saying he will still have thoughts and emotions like ours.

questions.explanation: After a long list of losses the speaker turns round and names what stays: future man will still be a human being, with thoughts and emotions similar to our own, and that reversal is the point the whole passage has been building towards. Saying he will not be human contradicts it word for word. Nothing at all is said about the voice, which is a change the passage never mentions. And far from admitting that nothing can be predicted, he opens by saying we can only guess but can be sure that man will be different — the guess is the argument, not a refusal to make one.
